author: CLOC · Harbor

sib.t: 2025 CLOC State of the Industry Report

dom.t: Legal departments: AI supports selective sourcing redesign

st.t: Legal departments: AI supports selective sourcing redesign
st.an: CLOC accepts the cluster’s operating-model framing and materially develops it by prescribing benchmarking as a basis for allocating resources, selecting AI-enabled workflows and establishing governance. It also interprets constrained spending and rising demand as an opportunity to strengthen legal operations rather than simply reduce headcount or external support.
qs: Benchmarking data can help make a strategic case to the C-suite about where to direct precious resources, and which tasks would derive the greatest benefit from applying AI-enabled workflows.
Far from contraction, we have entered a period of opportunity where legal operations drives cross-functional collaboration and value.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s work-redesign proposition and materially extends it with survey-based evidence from corporate legal departments: rising demand, constrained hiring and spending, and accelerating AI adoption are making technology, governance and legal operations central to operating-model change. It does not directly assess jagged task capability or verification.
qs: Rather than advancing previous discourse about "doing more with less," rising demand paired with tighter growth expectations is reshaping how legal departments operate, with technology and governance playing a larger role in how work gets done.
In this environment, legal operations is rising in strategic importance, becoming a main lever for efficiency at scale and enterprise success.

kp.k: Demand rises as traditional capacity options tighten
kp.d: Drawing on the 2025 Harbor Law Department Survey conducted with CLOC, the author reports surging demand in regulatory compliance, cybersecurity and complex contracting, while legal departments face greater constraints on adding headcount or sending work to outside counsel.
qs: The data from our 2025 Law Department Survey, conducted in collaboration with CLOC, reveals a legal operations ecosystem under strain.
Demand continues to surge in high-risk areas, such as regulatory compliance, cybersecurity, and complex contracting.
Yet, the most common relief valves — expanding headcount and offloading work to outside counsel — are more constrained than last year.

kp.k: Expected internal and external spending growth declines
kp.d: The survey reports that the share expecting increased outside-counsel spending fell from 58% in the prior year to 37%, while the share anticipating higher internal legal-department budgets fell from 65% to 47%. These are respondents' spending expectations rather than reported expenditure reductions.
qs: Expectations for increased spending on outside counsel have dropped sharply, from 58% last year to just 37% this year.

Projections of inside legal department spending follow a similar downward trajectory, with fewer than half of responding departments anticipating internal budget increases (47%), compared to 65% last year.

kp.k: AI adoption advances toward enterprise deployment
kp.d: The author characterizes legal departments as moving beyond experimentation toward intentional piloting and enterprise-level deployment of AI across several functions, despite flattening expectations for hiring and spending.
qs: The latest data poses a paradox: accelerating AI adoption comes at the same time that hiring and spending are leveling off.
Instead, legal departments are taking an intentional approach to adopting AI, piloting and deploying tools in multiple areas, from research to content creation to contracting and beyond.
We're seeing a decisive move from AI experimentation to enterprise-level deployment.

kp.k: Most departments establish dedicated AI governance
kp.d: The report states that 85% of departments have a dedicated resource or committee managing AI use, indicating that organizational governance is accompanying adoption. The document also recommends alignment on tools and policies supporting responsible AI use.
qs: At 85%, an overwhelming majority of departments now have a dedicated resource or committee in place to manage AI use.

Crucially, a data-backed approach can help win the buy-in you need to align on key decisions, such as the tools and governance policies needed to support the responsible use of AI based on industry practices.

kp.k: Legal operations uses AI across core workflows
kp.d: The author reports that legal operations professionals are applying AI to workflow support, legal research and efficiency, with the broader adoption scope also including content creation and contracting.
qs: Increasingly, legal ops professionals are relying on AI to help support workflows, accelerate research, and drive efficiencies.
Instead, legal departments are taking an intentional approach to adopting AI, piloting and deploying tools in multiple areas, from research to content creation to contracting and beyond.

kp.k: Legal operations gains greater strategic importance
kp.d: Under conditions of rising demand and constrained spending, the author argues that legal operations is becoming a principal mechanism for scalable efficiency and enterprise performance rather than merely an administrative support function.
qs: In this environment, legal operations is rising in strategic importance, becoming a main lever for efficiency at scale and enterprise success.
Far from contraction, we have entered a period of opportunity where legal operations drives cross-functional collaboration and value.

kp.k: Benchmarking informs AI and resource allocation
kp.d: The document recommends using industry benchmarking to support C-suite decisions about scarce resources and identify tasks likely to benefit from AI-enabled workflows. It presents data as a way to validate staffing ratios and technology spending and to show whether a department differs from peers.
qs: Benchmarking data can help make a strategic case to the C-suite about where to direct precious resources, and which tasks would derive the greatest benefit from applying AI-enabled workflows.
For example, the report can help validate the strategy for staffing ratios and technology spend by showing your department is not an outlier.

kp.k: Automation may redirect talent toward judgment-based work
kp.d: The author argues that benchmarking can reveal where senior talent performs high-volume work suitable for automation, allowing departments to accelerate service delivery and redirect internal capacity toward work requiring judgment. This is presented as a potential benefit and recommended strategy, not a measured workforce outcome.
qs: It can also identify gaps where high-level talent may be bogged down in high-volume tasks that have potential for automation.
With these insights and support from the data, you can focus on accelerating service delivery and freeing up internal resources for judgment-based work that delivers real value.

kp.k: Survey evidence spans organizations, industries and regions
kp.d: The hub page says the CLOC report provides insights from 135 organizations across industries and regions. It separately describes the underlying Harbor Law Department Survey, then in its 22nd year, as including data from more than 200 participating companies across more than 15 industries and covering spending, staffing, operations, technology, outside-counsel management and compensation.
qs: The CLOC State of the Industry Report is based on the Harbor Law Department Survey and delivers insights from 135 organizations across industries and regions.
The survey, now in its 22nd year, continues to expand its focus on global legal function management, including data from 200+ participating companies representing over 15 industries.

The annual Harbor Law Department Survey is the leading source of benchmarking data for corporate law departments, providing comprehensive data on legal spending, staffing, operations, technology, outside counsel management, and compensation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kevin Clem describes corporate legal departments moving from AI experimentation toward enterprise deployment, using AI to support workflows, accelerate research and improve efficiency.
pts.d: Clem attributes this shift to the latest Harbor Law Department Survey findings, describing adoption across research, content creation and contracting. He places accelerating adoption alongside rising demand and tighter expectations for hiring and spending; he does not establish that AI caused those budget constraints. His account emphasizes AI support for legal operations rather than autonomous replacement of lawyers.

pts.k: Clem argues that benchmarking-guided automation can accelerate legal service delivery and free internal talent for judgment-based work, while supporting decisions about responsible AI governance.
pts.d: This is a conditional opportunity and strategic recommendation, not a quantified finding about realized productivity. Clem proposes using industry benchmarking to locate high-volume tasks suitable for automation, make resource-allocation cases to executives and secure agreement on AI tools and governance policies. The contemplated change is a redistribution of internal work away from automatable tasks toward judgment-intensive activities.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is organizational survey data, including an 85% AI-governance figure and falling proportions expecting spending increases; the excerpt supplies no measured AI productivity gains.
pts.d: Clem identifies the 2025 Harbor Law Department Survey, conducted with CLOC, as the basis for his account. He reports that 85% of departments have a dedicated AI resource or committee. Expectations for increased outside-counsel spending fall from 58% to 37%, and expectations for internal budget increases fall from 65% to 47%; these measure spending expectations, not actual spending reductions or AI-caused savings. The hub describes the CLOC report as drawing on 135 organizations, separately describing the broader Harbor survey as including 200+ companies across more than 15 industries. The supplied text does not explain the relationship between these populations or provide question-level denominators, deployment rates, task-performance measurements or detailed transformation cases. Real-world examples are promised for a webinar rather than presented here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The adoption claims describe a current transition in a March 2, 2026 article based on 2025 survey data; prospective efficiency benefits have no specified delivery date.
pts.d: Clem uses present-tense language to describe enterprise deployment and compares spending expectations with the preceding survey year, without explicitly identifying the calendar years behind 'last year' and 'this year.' The proposed benefits depend on identifying suitable high-volume tasks, directing resources to AI-enabled workflows and securing organizational support for tools and governance. The setting is sustained demand in high-risk legal work with more constrained headcount expansion and outsourcing. The article does not predict a date for full deployment, lawyer replacement or a particular magnitude of savings.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, legal operations professionals, internal legal talent and executive decision-makers.
pts.d: Clem portrays legal operations as gaining strategic importance through technology deployment, workflow improvement and AI governance. Internal legal talent may be released from high-volume work to focus on judgment-based tasks; executives are asked to allocate resources and approve tools and policies using benchmarking evidence. Outside counsel appears as a constrained outsourcing option and a spending category, not as the subject of an explicit AI-displacement prediction. The source makes no specific claims about public access to justice, law-firm staffing structures or AI vendors' market shares.
